question: When you let a saved colour go on a row in the layers list, what should it paint?
context: A saved text style can already be dropped straight onto a row in the layers list. A saved colour cannot: aim a colour tile at a row and nothing happens and nothing is said. The reason it was left out is that a row is not a colour well. A well is labelled with the one thing it paints; a row carries only the layer's name, and a layer can have several colours (a button has a fill, an edge and its words) or none at all (a screenshot, a plain group). So letting go on a row needs a rule for which colour it lands on, and that rule is what you are choosing here. The line under the layers list already says out loud what a drop would do before you let go, which is what keeps any of these from being silent.

options.label: Its main colour, named before you let go
options.summary: The colour paints the one part the layer leads with, and the line under the list names that part while the tile is still in the air: "Paints Fill with Brand" over a box, "Paints Text with Brand" over words, "Paints Line with Brand" over an arrow, "Paints Border with Brand" over a screenshot that wears a ring. A screenshot with no ring and a plain group say "Screenshot has no colour to paint." and stay dark.
pros: It is the same part the Appearance section already leads with, so the list and the inspector agree
Nothing is silent: the part is named before you let go, and a row that cannot take a colour says why
For almost every layer there is only one part anyway, so there is nothing to be surprised by
cons: An arrow with a coloured head gets a recoloured shaft and keeps its old head, which can look half done
To paint a part that is not the main one you still go to the inspector
options.mitigation: The sentence says exactly which part before the pointer is let go, so the half-done arrow is visible as a choice rather than a surprise, and letting go somewhere else costs nothing.

options.label: Everything the layer paints
options.summary: One drop makes the whole layer that colour. Over a button the fill, the edge and the words all go Brand at once, and the line reads "Paints all 3 colours of Save button with Brand."
pros: No guessing about which part: the answer is all of them
Fast for the case people ask for most, making one thing one colour
cons: Words and their background both going Brand leaves text you cannot read
It quietly throws away colour work you already did on the other parts
The more parts a layer has, the more the drop does that you did not ask for
options.mitigation: It is one undo step, so it is always one keystroke back.

options.label: The row opens so you can pick the part
options.summary: Holding a colour over a row unfolds it into its parts, the way a group row opens, and you let go on the one you mean: Fill, Border, Text. A layer with only one part opens into one line.
pros: You always say which part, so nothing is ever chosen for you
It reaches parts that are not the main one without leaving the list
cons: The list moves under the pointer mid drag, which is the thing a drag is worst at
Two steps for the one part case, which is nearly every layer
It is a second, smaller copy of the inspector living inside the layers list
options.mitigation: The unfold could be held back until the pointer has rested on the row for a moment, so a colour crossing the list on its way somewhere else never disturbs it.

options.label: Leave colour off the layers list
options.summary: A colour tile keeps going only to the colour wells in the inspector, where the well says what it paints. Aiming one at a layer row shows the no entry sign, as it does today.
pros: No new rule to learn, and no chance of painting a part you did not mean
The layers list stays about picking, naming and ordering layers
cons: Saved text styles CAN be dropped on a row, so the list takes one kind of tile and refuses the other with no visible reason
Recolouring a layer you are not currently editing still means selecting it and losing what you had picked
options.mitigation: The inspector well is one extra click away, and clicking a saved colour in a row menu still does the same job.
